analogy.p: Imagine a tall building with a heater in the basement so the basement is warm and the roof is cold. Imagine each hydrocarbon is a person who is carried upwards by warm air but will only 'settle' on the first floor that is cooler than their personal comfort temperature. Heavy, long-chain 'people' (high boiling point) settle on the low floors, which are still warm, while light, short-chain 'people' (low boiling point) travel all the way to the top. This is how fractions condense at different heights. The analogy breaks down because molecules do not choose where to go: they condense purely because the temperature drops below their boiling point.
analogy.t: A tall building with a heater in the basement

bullets: Crude oil is a **mixture** of hydrocarbons that are **not chemically combined**.
Separation is **physical**: no new substances are made and the molecules are not changed.
Each part of the mixture needs different properties for its job (a jet fuel and a road surface need very different molecules).
The molecules in crude oil have **different chain lengths**, which gives them **different boiling points**.
Fractional distillation separates a mixture of **liquids with different boiling points**.
Crude oil is processed continuously at an **oil refinery**.
Link: simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution; fractional distillation separates **several** liquids.
core.h: Why crude oil must be separated
core.p: Crude oil is a **mixture** of hydrocarbons, most of them **alkanes**, with chains of many different lengths. In this raw form it is a thick, dark liquid that is not much use: you cannot put it straight into a car engine, and the different molecules behave differently. By separating the mixture into groups of molecules of similar size we obtain useful products. Because the compounds in crude oil are not chemically joined, separation needs only a **physical method**, and the method chosen is **fractional distillation**, which uses the differences in **boiling point**.

bullets: A fraction is a **mixture of hydrocarbons with a similar number of carbon atoms** and a similar boiling range.
The main fractions from top to bottom: **refinery gases (liquefied petroleum gases), petrol, kerosene, diesel oil, fuel oil (heavy fuel oil), bitumen**.
Refinery gases are the **smallest** molecules (up to about 4 carbons); bitumen has the **largest**.
Each fraction has a **range** of boiling points, not a single value.
Fractions can be used as they are, or processed further (for example by **cracking**).
The names petrol, kerosene and diesel describe the use as well as the chemistry.
Exam tip: say 'a mixture of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points', not 'a pure compound'.
core.p: A **fraction** is a group of hydrocarbons in crude oil that have **similar chain lengths** and therefore **similar boiling points**. Fractional distillation does not give pure compounds; each fraction is itself a mixture of hydrocarbons with a similar number of carbon atoms. The fractions are named after how they are used, for example petrol or diesel oil. Fractions with short chains collect at the top of the column and those with long chains collect at the bottom.

bullets: Step 1: crude oil is **heated until it evaporates** (vaporised).
Step 2: the vapour enters the **fractionating column**, which has a **temperature gradient**: hot at the bottom, cooler at the top.
Step 3: vapours **rise** up the column and **cool**.
Step 4: each hydrocarbon **condenses** at the level where the temperature is below its boiling point.
Step 5: liquids are collected from **trays** at different heights as fractions.
Step 6: molecules with **short chains / low boiling points** are drawn off at the **top**; **long chains / high boiling points** near the **bottom**.
Step 7: the thick residue (**bitumen**) is not vaporised and is taken from the bottom.
This is a **continuous** process: oil is fed in all the time and products removed all the time.
core.p: The industrial process takes place in a tall **fractionating column**. First the crude oil is **heated** in a furnace so that most of it **evaporates**. The hot vapour is fed into the **bottom** of the column. The column is **hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top**. As the vapours rise they cool. Each hydrocarbon **condenses** when it reaches a height where the temperature is **just below its boiling point**, and it is then drawn off as a liquid. Molecules with the **lowest boiling points** reach the top and leave as gases, while the **largest molecules** with the highest boiling points condense near the bottom or stay as a thick liquid.

bullets: The **bottom** of the column is the **hottest** part; the **top** is the **coolest**.
Vapour **rises** because it is hot and gaseous.
A substance **condenses when the temperature is below its boiling point**.
High boiling point → condenses **lower down**; low boiling point → condenses **higher up**.
Gases such as the refinery gases are still gases at the top and are **drawn off as gases**.
The largest molecules may not evaporate at all and **stay at the bottom**.
Trays or plates at different heights **collect** the liquids that have condensed.
core.h: Why there is a temperature gradient in the column
core.p: The column is heated from the bottom by the incoming hot vapour and the furnace, and it loses heat as you go up, so the bottom is hotter than the top. This gradient is what allows separation. A hydrocarbon with a high boiling point can condense low in the column where it is still quite hot, because the temperature there is below its boiling point. A hydrocarbon with a low boiling point only condenses where the column is very cool, so it travels much higher. Examiners like the phrase 'condenses when the temperature falls below its boiling point'.

bullets: **Refinery gases**: heating and cooking (e.g. bottled gas).
**Petrol**: fuel for cars.
**Kerosene**: fuel for aircraft.
**Diesel oil**: fuel for some cars, lorries and trains.
**Fuel oil**: fuel for large ships and for some power stations.
**Bitumen**: surfacing roads and roofs.
**Feedstock** for the petrochemical industry: solvents, lubricants, polymers, detergents.
Mnemonic idea for the order (top to bottom): **G**ood **P**eople **K**eep **D**oing **F**ractions **B**etter — make up your own, but learn the order.
core.h: The fractions, their order and uses
core.p: Remember the order from the top of the column to the bottom: **refinery gases, petrol, kerosene, diesel oil, fuel oil, bitumen**. As you go **down** the column the molecules get **longer**. Most fractions are burned as **fuels**: refinery gases (liquefied petroleum gases) in cooking and heating, petrol in cars, kerosene in aircraft, diesel oil in lorries, trains and some cars, and fuel oil in ships and power stations. Some of the fractions are used as **feedstock** for the **petrochemical industry**, providing the starting materials for making **solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents**. **Bitumen** is used to surface roads and roofs.

bullets: **Boiling point increases** as chain length increases.
**Viscosity increases**: longer chains are thicker and flow less easily.
**Flammability decreases**: longer chains are harder to ignite.
**Volatility decreases**: longer chains evaporate less easily (so are less likely to form a vapour).
Shortest chains (methane to butane) are **gases at room temperature**; medium chains are **liquids**; the longest are **thick liquids or solids**.
Trends are **gradual**, which is why a homologous series is useful for predicting properties.
Data questions: always give the trend and then **quote values** from the table or graph.
core.h: Trends in properties as chain length increases
core.p: The physical properties of hydrocarbons change in a regular way with the **length of the carbon chain**. As the molecules get **larger** the **boiling point increases**, the liquid becomes **more viscous** (it flows less easily, like treacle), it becomes **less flammable** (harder to ignite) and **less volatile** (it evaporates less easily). These patterns decide which fraction is used for which job. Short-chain fractions such as petrol are runny, easy to ignite and boil at low temperatures. Long-chain fractions like bitumen are thick, hard to ignite and boil at high temperatures.

bullets: Boiling is the **overcoming of intermolecular forces**, not the breaking of covalent bonds.
**Larger molecules** → **stronger intermolecular forces** → **more energy** needed → **higher boiling point**.
Stronger intermolecular forces also make the liquid **more viscous**.
Smaller molecules have weak forces, so petrol and gases **evaporate easily** and ignite easily.
Mark-scheme words: 'intermolecular forces', 'more energy needed to overcome', 'larger molecules'.
Do not write 'covalent bonds break': it loses marks.
This idea also explains why simple molecular substances have low melting/boiling points compared with giant structures.
core.h: Explaining the trend: intermolecular forces (Higher tier link)
core.p: Why does boiling point rise with chain length? When a liquid boils you are **not breaking the covalent bonds** inside the molecules; you are overcoming the **intermolecular forces** between molecules. Longer molecules have a larger surface and more electrons, so the forces between neighbouring molecules are **stronger**. More energy is needed to separate them, so the boiling point is higher. This is the same reasoning used for **simple molecular substances** in the bonding topic. A high-quality answer says 'bigger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, which need more energy to overcome', and never says 'covalent bonds break'.

bullets: **Complete combustion**: hydrocarbon + oxygen → **carbon dioxide + water** (plus energy).
Both **carbon and hydrogen are oxidised** (they gain oxygen).
Methane: **CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O**.
Propane: **C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O**.
Combustion is **exothermic**: energy is released to the surroundings.
Incomplete combustion (limited oxygen) can form **carbon monoxide** and **carbon (soot)** instead; this is covered in the atmosphere topic.
Fuels burn in the **gas phase**: more volatile fuels ignite more easily.
core.p: Hydrocarbon fuels release energy when they **burn** (combust) in oxygen. In **complete combustion** with plenty of oxygen, both the carbon and the hydrogen in the fuel are **oxidised**: carbon becomes **carbon dioxide** and hydrogen becomes **water**. Energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the reaction is **exothermic**. The word equation is: hydrocarbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. For methane the balanced symbol equation is CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. Oxidation here means the **gain of oxygen**.

bullets: Step 1: write the unbalanced equation, e.g. C3H8 + O2 → CO2 + H2O.
Step 2: balance **C**: 3 C so **3CO2**.
Step 3: balance **H**: 8 H so **4H2O**.
Step 4: count **O** on the right: 3 x 2 + 4 = 10, so **5O2** on the left.
Step 5: check each element has the same count on both sides.
If you get a half (e.g. C2H6 needs 3.5 O2) **multiply everything by 2**: 2C2H6 + 7O2 → 4CO2 + 6H2O.
Never change a formula to balance, only the **numbers in front**.
core.p: Balancing equations is a method skill. Start with the **carbon**, then the **hydrogen**, and finally the **oxygen**, because oxygen appears in two products and is easily adjusted last. For each carbon in the fuel you need one CO2. For every two hydrogens you need one H2O. Then count all the oxygen atoms on the right and divide by two to give the number of O2 molecules. If the answer is a fraction, double everything.

bullets: **Simple distillation**: for a solvent from a solution (e.g. water from salt water).
**Fractional distillation**: for **mixtures of liquids** with different boiling points (e.g. ethanol and water, crude oil).
In the lab, the column is filled with **glass beads** to provide a large surface area for condensation.
The **thermometer** is at the top of the column and shows the boiling point of the fraction leaving.
Collect samples in different containers as the temperature rises.
Safety: heat flammable liquids with a **water bath or electric heater, not a naked flame**; wear eye protection.
Industrial: **continuous**, huge scale, with a **temperature gradient** rather than a fixed lab temperature.
core.h: Fractional distillation versus simple distillation, and in the lab
core.p: **Simple distillation** separates a liquid from a solution or from a mixture where the boiling points are very different. **Fractional distillation** is used when the liquids have **similar boiling points**, so a fractionating column is added. In a lab model of the process, a mixture of liquids is heated in a flask with a fractionating column above it (filled with glass beads to give a large surface for condensing and re-evaporating) and a thermometer measures the temperature of the vapour; the substance with the lowest boiling point reaches the condenser first and is collected. The industrial column works on the same principle but with a continuous temperature gradient.

bullets: Demand is highest for **short-chain fuels**, such as petrol and diesel.
Crude oil contains many **long-chain** molecules for which demand is lower.
**Cracking** breaks long hydrocarbons into short, more useful ones (next topic).
The alkenes from cracking are **feedstock** for polymers.
Fractional distillation is a **physical** process; cracking is a **chemical** process.
Fractions can be **blended** to make fuels of the right quality.
Exam tip: link supply and demand to cracking in 'why is cracking needed?' questions.
core.h: Supply, demand and link to cracking
core.p: Crude oil does not contain the fractions in the same proportions as we need them. There are **more long-chain hydrocarbons** than the market wants, and **short-chain hydrocarbons** such as petrol are in higher demand. The refinery therefore uses **cracking** to convert surplus long-chain molecules into shorter, more useful alkanes and alkenes. Fractional distillation is the first step; cracking is the second and is the next topic. Understanding this chain explains why oil companies do more than just distil.

bullets: **Carbon dioxide** from complete combustion adds to the **greenhouse effect**.
**Carbon monoxide** is a toxic gas from incomplete combustion.
**Sulfur dioxide** from sulfur impurities causes acid rain (Atmosphere topic).
Crude oil is **finite**; using it for fuel reduces supply for **feedstock**.
Alternatives include biofuels, hydrogen and electricity from renewable sources.
Evaluate: advantages (energy-dense, convenient, established) versus disadvantages (pollution, finite).
Always end an evaluation with a **clear judgement** supported by evidence.
core.p: Burning hydrocarbon fuels releases **carbon dioxide** (a greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming) and, if combustion is incomplete, **carbon monoxide** and **soot**. Fuels containing **sulfur** impurities release sulfur dioxide, which causes acid rain. Crude oil is also a **finite** resource, so using it as fuel means it is no longer available as a feedstock for making plastics and other materials. In 6-mark questions you may be asked to evaluate using fractions as fuels compared with alternatives; make a balanced argument and finish with a conclusion.

bullets: Formed from the remains of **ancient biomass, mainly plankton**, buried in mud over millions of years.
A **mixture of hydrocarbons** (hydrogen and carbon only), most of which are **alkanes**.
**Finite and non-renewable**: used faster than it forms.
Alkanes are **saturated** hydrocarbons: every carbon-carbon bond is a single covalent bond.
Alkanes form the **homologous series** with general formula **CnH2n+2**.
First four alkanes: **methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10**.
Crude oil is a mixture, so each hydrocarbon keeps its **own properties** and can be separated physically.
Crude oil gives **fuels** and **feedstock** for the petrochemical industry (polymers, solvents, lubricants, detergents).
core.h: Where crude oil comes from and what it is made of
core.p: **Crude oil** is a finite resource found in rocks. It formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient **plankton** (tiny sea creatures) that were buried in mud, then subjected to heat and pressure. It is a mixture of many different **hydrocarbons**, compounds made of hydrogen and carbon atoms only, and most of them are **alkanes**. Because it takes millions of years to form and we use it much faster than it is made, crude oil is described as **non-renewable** and finite. This is why separating and using it carefully matters, both as fuel and as the raw material for the petrochemical industry.

bullets: **CnH2n+2**: methane n=1 gives CH4; ethane n=2 gives C2H6; propane n=3 gives C3H8; butane n=4 gives C4H10.
Pentane C5H12, hexane C6H14, heptane C7H16, octane C8H18.
Names have a stem for the carbon count: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-, hept-, oct-.
The suffix **-ane** shows a saturated hydrocarbon (alkane).
Each extra carbon adds **CH2**, so neighbouring members differ by one CH2 unit.
Chemical properties are **similar** through the series; physical properties change gradually.
You can draw displayed formulae with every C-H and C-C single bond shown.
Check a formula by counting hydrogen atoms: it must equal 2n+2.
core.h: Alkane formulae and naming (links to the diagrams)
core.p: The specification expects you to recognise that alkanes follow the general formula **CnH2n+2**, so a chain with n carbon atoms has 2n+2 hydrogen atoms. The names of the first four come from methane, ethane, propane and butane, and the next ones are pentane, hexane, heptane and octane (C5 to C8). The figures on this note use these molecules to show how chain length controls boiling point: more carbon atoms means a larger molecule with more surface in contact with its neighbours, so stronger intermolecular forces. Practise writing the formula from the number of carbons, for example octane has n = 8 so C8H18.

exam: 'Describe how fractional distillation separates crude oil' (4-6 marks): heated and evaporated; vapour enters column; temperature gradient (hot at bottom, cool at top); vapours rise and condense at their boiling points; short chains at the top, long chains at the bottom; fractions drawn off.
Use the key phrase 'condenses when the temperature is below its boiling point'.
'State the trend' questions: write the direction clearly, e.g. 'as chain length increases, boiling point increases'.
Data and graph questions: quote two data values from the table or graph to support a trend (e.g. 'boiling point rises from -162 °C to 126 °C').
'Explain why boiling point increases with chain length' (Higher, 2-3 marks): larger molecules, stronger intermolecular forces, more energy needed to overcome them.
Do not say 'bonds break' for boiling; say 'intermolecular forces'.
Combustion equations (2-3 marks): write the correct formulae first, then balance; 1 mark for formulae, 1 for balance.
'Complete combustion' product pairs: carbon dioxide and water; if the question says 'limited oxygen' think carbon monoxide or carbon.
Fraction uses (1 mark each): match each fraction to a fuel use (e.g. kerosene – aircraft, bitumen – roads).
6-mark evaluation: give advantages and disadvantages, link to chain length and to environmental effects, and finish with a justified conclusion.

mistakes.w: Fractional distillation separates crude oil by melting point or by size using a filter.

mistakes.r: Each fraction is a mixture of hydrocarbons with similar chain lengths and boiling points.
mistakes.w: Each fraction is a pure compound.

mistakes.r: Boiling overcomes the weak intermolecular forces between molecules; the covalent bonds stay intact.
mistakes.w: The covalent bonds break when a hydrocarbon boils.

mistakes.r: The column is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top.
mistakes.w: The column is hotter at the top.

mistakes.r: Bigger molecules have higher boiling points, are more viscous and less flammable.
mistakes.w: Bigger molecules are more flammable and runnier.

mistakes.r: Bitumen has the highest boiling point so it is collected at the bottom.
mistakes.w: Bitumen comes off at the top because it is heavy.

mistakes.r: Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water.
Only the large numbers in front of formulae can be changed when balancing.
mistakes.w: Balancing by changing the formula, e.g. CO3.

mistakes.r: A vapour condenses when its temperature falls below its boiling point.
mistakes.w: Condensation happens because the vapour 'wants' to go back.

summary: Crude oil is separated into useful fractions by fractional distillation, which works because the hydrocarbons have different boiling points. You must describe the process, name the main fractions and their uses, explain how boiling point, viscosity and flammability change with chain length, and write equations for the complete combustion of hydrocarbons. This links bonding, energy and the fuels we depend on.

terms.d: A method of separating a mixture of liquids with different boiling points by evaporating them and condensing them at different temperatures in a fractionating column.
A mixture of hydrocarbons with similar chain lengths and similar boiling points, separated from crude oil.
A tall tower, hot at the bottom and cooler at the top, in which crude oil vapours rise and condense at different heights.
The change from liquid to gas at the surface of a liquid; here the oil is heated until it vaporises.
The change from gas to liquid when a vapour is cooled below its boiling point.
The temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas throughout the liquid.
How easily a liquid flows; a viscous liquid is thick and flows slowly.
How easily a substance catches fire.
How easily a liquid evaporates; volatile liquids have low boiling points.
Weak forces of attraction between molecules; they are overcome when a simple molecular substance melts or boils.
The fraction with the smallest molecules (liquefied petroleum gases), used for heating and cooking.
The fraction with the largest molecules, a thick residue used to surface roads and roofs.
A raw material for an industrial process, such as the petrochemical industry making polymers.
Burning in plenty of oxygen so that carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide and hydrogen to water.
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
A saturated hydrocarbon with only single bonds and general formula CnH2n+2.
A compound made of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
A family of compounds with the same general formula and similar chemical properties.

worked.ans: The oil is heated so it evaporates and the vapour enters the bottom of a fractionating column that is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top. The vapours rise and each condenses where the temperature drops below its boiling point, so hydrocarbons with short chains and low boiling points are collected at the top, while those with long chains and high boiling points are collected near the bottom.
worked.q: Describe how crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: crude oil is heated until it evaporates / is vaporised.
Mark 2: vapour enters the fractionating column, which is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top.
Mark 3: vapours rise and each hydrocarbon condenses where the temperature falls below its boiling point.
Mark 4: short-chain (low boiling point) fractions leave at the top; long-chain (high boiling point) fractions near the bottom.

worked.q: The table gives boiling points: pentane 36 °C, hexane 69 °C, octane 126 °C. Describe the trend and explain it. Which is most viscous? (3 marks)
steps: Trend: boiling point increases as the number of carbon atoms increases (36 → 69 → 126 °C).
Explanation: larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to overcome them.
Viscosity increases with chain length, so octane is the most viscous.
